newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's doctors adapt to media glare.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's doctors adapt to media glare.

text.p: Doctors treating Mother Teresa have to cope with the stress of caring for an 86-year-old ailing icon, but also the constant glare of the media.
Dozens of news organisations have kept a vigil over the eight-member team of doctors since the revered Roman Catholic nun was taken to hospital with heart failure on November 22.
The doctors say they derive special satisfaction out of caring for the 1979 Nobel peace prize winner and take the media attention in stride.
Dr Tarun Praharaj, who performed life-saving surgery on Mother Teresa on November 29, said the media interest was just another facet of his high-pressure job.

"Dealing with the intense press interest is not actually part of my job, but in my job you do learn to handle stress," Praharaj told Reuters in the eastern Indian city of Calcutta. "So it's just another thing to deal with."
Praharaj said there was something special about treating Mother Teresa, known around the world for her life-long devotion to the poor and the sick.
"No one like her has ever been seen in the world," he said.
Praharaj performed an angioplasty procedure on Mother Teresa to clear two blocked coronary arteries. He placed a balloon in each blood vessel and then inflated it to clear the passage.
"It is always satisfying to see patients make progress," Praharaj said. "In Mother Teresa's case, even more so."
Praharaj works at the B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre, which puts out four daily updates on Mother Teresa's condition.
With spiky red hair and aviator-like spectacles, he handles questions from the press deftly, his expertise belying a boyish appearance.

The 37-year-old cardiologist said he trained in Manila, New York's Mount Sinai hospital and Zurich before launching his six-year-old practice at the Birla clinic. Praharaj also performed an angioplasty on Mother Teresa at Birla in 1993.
Doctors said Mother Teresa was having difficulty shaking off bronchial pneumonia, which she contracted when long-standing lung and kidney problems resurfaced soon after the surgery.
Another member of the team is the stern, raven-haired American Dr Patricia Aubanel. Her style of dealing with the media contrasts with Praharaj's.
"You should be happy you're getting four bulletins a day," she told reporters recently. "In my country there's just one."
Last week she disagreed with Praharaj over the time it would take Mother Teresa to recover, saying she might be home soon. The nun's stay has since been prolonged.
Aubanel works at the Scripps La Jolla clinic in California. She first treated Mother Teresa in 1991, doing an angioplasty on her in the United States. The two have formed a strong bond.
"Ever since then, she flies down and gives Mother Teresa a free check-up every six months," one official said. "She does it at her own expense, wherever Mother is."
Aubanel and Dr Bernarda Lara, a Mexican intensive care specialist, keep close watch over Mother Teresa's condition.
"Mother Teresa prefers a lady doctor over a man doctor," clinic official A.K. Chatterjee said.
"Dr Aubanel knows the details of her body chemistry. It is easier for her to understand, grasp the situation and take instant remedial measures."
